meta.blurb: Lina says yes to everyone and no to herself. Her aunt Rosa, a tailor, teaches her an old idea: what people think of you is their business, and what you do is yours. Join Lina as she learns to be kind, honest and free.
meta.bible: Lina: a woman of twenty-six who works in an office and says yes to everyone; tired, kind and anxious to be liked. Rosa: Lina's aunt, a tailor with a small shop on Mill Lane; warm, direct and funny. Lina's mother: loving and worried, hopes Lina will keep her steady job. Mei: Lina's friend from school, who drifts away. Mr Hale: Lina's manager at the insurance office. The two gardens: Rosa's picture for the idea that your garden holds your choices and actions, and other people's gardens hold their thoughts and opinions. The sewing class: an evening class in clothes design that Lina joins. Key ideas, one per beat: belonging, approval, imagining what others think, the spotlight effect (people notice us less than we think, supported by research, hedged), the cost of saying yes, saying no kindly, guilt, family hopes, social media, comparison, sorting criticism, values, fear of being disliked, friends who stay, grief, responsibility, courage, self-respect, contribution. Voice: warm, honest, practical, gently funny; never harsh and never preachy. This is not about ignoring everyone: good advice is still worth hearing. No invented studies, numbers or quotes.

beats.summary: Lina, who says yes to everything, is exhausted at midnight doing other people's tasks.

beats.scene: Early people sit around a fire at night, one gazing into the dark

beats.scene: Rosa kneels beside two garden plots separated by a low fence
beats.summary: Rosa's two gardens: your garden holds your actions and choices; theirs holds their thoughts.

beats.summary: You cannot control what people think, but you can control what you do.

beats.scene: Lina holds an empty cup out hopefully to a crowd who walk past

beats.scene: A friend frowns slightly at Lina, then looks out of a window

beats.scene: Lina sits on the edge of her bed holding her chest, looking uneasy

beats.scene: Lina's mother looks out of a window with a gentle, thoughtful expression

beats.scene: Lina looks at two shelves, one tidy and glowing and one messy but real

beats.scene: Lina listens with an open notebook as an older colleague gives advice

beats.scene: Lina greets a customer warmly while firmly refusing a poor discount

B1B2: It is midnight, and Lina is still at her kitchen table doing work for other people. She has said yes to every request this week, and she has not said yes to herself once.
On Saturday Lina visits her aunt Rosa, who has a tailor's shop on Mill Lane. Rosa looks at her niece's tired face and says she looks like a coat with too many buttons.
Rosa says it is natural to care what others think. Long ago, people who were pushed out of the group were in real danger, so the wish to belong is very old.
Rosa explains that caring about others is good and kind. The problem begins when other people's opinions become the rules that run your life.
Rosa asks Lina to write down whose opinions she worries about. The list is long, and it includes her mother, her manager, her friends and even strangers online.
Rosa draws a small circle and a big one. In the small circle are the few people whose views matter, and in the big circle are all the others, whose views matter much less.
Rosa tells Lina a story about two gardens beside a fence. Your own garden holds your own choices and actions, but another person's garden holds their thoughts about you, and only they can tend it.
Rosa says that Lina cannot control what other people think of her, however hard she tries. She can only choose what she does, and do it as well and kindly as she can.
As a small test, Lina gets a bold new haircut. A colleague says she preferred the old one, and Lina notices that she is perfectly fine afterwards.
Rosa tells her about something called the spotlight effect. Studies suggest that we tend to think others notice us more than they really do, because everyone is busy thinking about themselves.
Lina often feels sure that she knows what others think of her. Rosa asks how she can know, since she has never seen inside anyone's head.
Rosa says approval is like salty water, because the more you drink, the thirstier you become. Lina realises that no amount of praise has ever been enough.
Rosa asks Lina to count the cost of pleasing everybody. It takes her time, her energy and sometimes even her honesty, because she says what people want to hear.
Every yes to someone else is a no to something else, Rosa says. When Lina agrees out of habit, she may be giving up time that she really wants for herself.
Rosa gives Lina a useful sentence: let me think about it and come back to you. It gives her time to decide what she really wants, instead of agreeing in a panic.
Lina decides to practise with the smallest no that she can find. When a colleague asks her to cover a task, she says she is sorry but she cannot, and her heart beats very fast.
Rosa teaches her how to say no kindly: be warm, be short and be clear. A long excuse is not needed, and it often invites an argument.
Not everyone is happy when Lina says no to them. Rosa reminds her that being disappointed is a feeling that belongs to the other person, and they can look after it.
After she says no, Lina feels guilty about it afterwards. Rosa says guilt is a feeling, not proof of a crime, and that she should ask herself whether she really did anything wrong.
Lina's mother loves her very much, and she worries about her a great deal. She hopes that Lina will keep her steady job at the insurance office, because she thinks it is safe.
Rosa says that Lina can love her mother and still make different choices. Respect and obedience, she says, are not the same thing.
One evening Lina speaks to her mother calmly and kindly. She explains what she wants, thanks her for her worry, and says she has thought carefully about her choices.
Lina realises that her mother's fears come from love, not from a wish to control her. Over the next weeks, her mother slowly begins to listen and to ask questions.
Lina often counts the likes on her photographs soon after she posts them. Rosa says that likes turn opinions into numbers, and that numbers are a poor way to measure a person.
Lina often feels that other people's lives are better than hers. Rosa reminds her that people usually show only their best moments, so the comparison is not fair.
One afternoon Rosa tells Lina the story of her own young life. People said that tailoring was not a proper job for a clever girl, but she did it anyway.
Rosa gives Lina three questions for criticism: who is saying it, do they really know me, and is it useful? These questions help her to decide what to keep.
Lina worries that she will stop listening to anyone. Rosa says that good advice is still valuable, and that a wise person listens carefully before deciding for herself.
Lina learns that she can be honest without being unkind. A true word, said gently and at the right moment, can respect both the other person and herself.
Rosa asks Lina a question that nobody has asked her before: what matters most to you? After a long time Lina writes five values on a card, such as honesty, creativity, kindness, health and family.
Rosa says that values are like a compass for hard choices. When Lina has a hard decision to make, she can check whether the choice points toward the things she cares about.
Lina is afraid of being disliked, and Rosa suggests she faces this fear a little at a time. Each small step makes the fear a bit smaller.
At a dinner with friends, Lina says honestly which film she wants to see, and it is not the popular one. Nobody is angry, and one friend says she wanted to see it too.
Rosa tells her a hard truth: some people will dislike you, however kind you are. Trying to please everyone is impossible, so it is wiser to stop trying.
Lina notices that her closest friends are not upset when she says no. Real friends accept that she has her own life, and the right people stay.
One old friend, Mei, drifts away because she liked Lina better when she always said yes. Lina feels sad about this, and she lets herself feel it.
Rosa says that it is natural to grieve when something ends. Lina allows herself some sadness, and then notices what she has gained: more time, more truth and more peace.
Rosa reminds Lina that she can only do what is in her own garden. Each day she chooses one small task that is truly hers to do, and she does it well.
Lina often says she is shy because of how she was brought up. Rosa says the past can explain us, but it does not have to decide what we do next.
Lina knows that every choice has consequences, and some people may not like her choice. She decides to join an evening class in clothes design, and she signs her name.
At her first class, Lina is sure that everyone will watch her and judge her. In fact the others are busy with their own work, and several give her a friendly smile.
Lina's first sleeve comes out crooked, and she feels hot with embarrassment. Her classmate laughs kindly and shows her how to fix it, and soon the embarrassment is gone.
Lina decides to talk to her manager, Mr Hale. She prepares carefully and asks him politely for a workload that she can really manage.
Mr Hale is surprised, but he is not angry. He agrees to some of what Lina asks, and they decide to talk again in a month.
One colleague is annoyed that Lina no longer does her tasks. Lina feels uncomfortable, but she stays calm and remembers that the other person's feeling is in her own garden.
As weeks pass, Lina feels something new growing inside her, a quiet respect for herself. She does not need everyone's approval to feel that she matters.
Lina makes a scarf for an elderly neighbour as a gift. Giving because she wants to is very different from pleasing people because she is afraid not to.
Rosa says that being liked is pleasant, but being trusted is better. People trust those who tell the truth and keep their word, even when it is not what they want to hear.
A year after the class began, Lina finishes her first coat, designed and sewn by herself. It hangs in Rosa's shop window on Mill Lane, and passers-by stop to look.
Rosa says that the lesson is simple, though not easy: tend your own garden and let others tend theirs. Be kind, be honest and be brave, and let other people think what they will.
C1C2: At midnight Lina was still sitting at her kitchen table, finishing a report for a colleague, planning a party for a friend and answering a message from a cousin she hardly knew. She had said yes to every request that week without a moment's hesitation, because the idea of disappointing anyone made her stomach tighten. Not once, she realised with a sinking feeling, had she said yes to something that she herself wanted, and she could not remember the last time she had been asked.

On Saturday Lina visited her aunt Rosa, who ran a small tailor's shop on Mill Lane, among bolts of fabric and the smell of warm steam. Rosa took one look at her niece's grey face and announced, with her usual lack of ceremony, that she looked like a coat with too many buttons. Lina laughed, and then, to her own surprise, she began to cry in the warm and cluttered shop, while Rosa quietly put the kettle on.

It is perfectly natural to care what other people think, Rosa told her, because human beings have always lived in groups and long ago being pushed out of one could be dangerous. The wish to belong is therefore very old, and the fear of rejection may be partly a relic of those times, though this is a matter on which scientists offer different views. Lina was relieved to learn that her anxiety was not a personal failing but an old and very human habit of the mind.

Rosa explained that caring about other people is a virtue and not a fault, and that nobody would want to live without it. The trouble begins when their opinions stop being information and turn into rules that decide how we live, what we say and even what we dare to want. Freedom, she said, does not mean caring less about people, but letting them advise us without letting them govern us.

Rosa handed her a pencil and asked her to write down every person whose opinion she worried about, and the list grew alarmingly long. It included her mother, her manager, her oldest friends, the neighbours, her cousins and even strangers whose names she had never learned. Lina stared at the page and realised that she was carrying an entire crowd around with her.

Rosa drew two circles on a scrap of paper, one small and one very large, and explained that not all opinions deserve the same weight. In the small circle sit the few people who know you well, wish you well and have earned the right to advise you, while the large circle holds everyone else. Most of Lina's worrying, she suggested, was being done on behalf of the large circle.

Rosa described two gardens that sit side by side, separated only by a low wooden fence, and she asked Lina to picture them. In your own garden grow your choices and your actions, and these are yours to plant and weed, while in everyone else's garden grow their thoughts, including their thoughts about you, and these are theirs alone to tend. It is a mistake, she said, to spend your whole life leaning over the fence and pulling at their flowers.

The uncomfortable truth, Rosa said, is that you cannot control what other people think of you, however carefully you behave, since their thoughts grow in their own gardens according to their own weather. What you can do is choose your actions and carry them out as honestly and kindly as possible. Having done that, you have done your part, and the rest was never yours to manage.

As a small experiment, Lina had her hair cut shorter than she had ever dared, and she walked into the office feeling like a nervous explorer. One colleague remarked that she preferred the old style, and Lina waited for the world to end, but it carried on much as usual. She went to lunch, laughed at a joke and discovered that a disapproving comment is not, in fact, a catastrophe.

Rosa mentioned something that psychologists call the spotlight effect, the finding that people tend to overestimate how closely others observe them. Everyone, she pointed out, is the star of their own show and spends most of the day worrying about their own performance, so the audience is much more distracted than we fear. Lina found this oddly comforting, rather like discovering that the stage lights were switched off.

Lina admitted that she often felt certain she knew what people were thinking about her, usually something critical. Rosa asked, gently, how she could possibly know, since nobody had ever managed to see inside another person's head. Most of the opinions that frightened Lina, it turned out, were ones that she had written for other people herself.

Approval, Rosa told her, is like salty water: it feels as though it will quench your thirst, but each drink only makes you thirstier. Lina thought back over the compliments she had worked so hard to collect and realised that none of them had ever felt like enough for more than an afternoon. A hunger that can never be satisfied, she saw, is a poor master, and she had been obeying it for most of her adult life.

Rosa asked her to count what her constant pleasing actually cost, and the answer was sobering. It cost her evenings, her energy, her sleep, and, perhaps most seriously, her honesty, since she so often said what people wanted to hear instead of what she believed. These were expensive prices to pay for the fleeting warmth of someone's good opinion.

Every yes, Rosa observed, contains a hidden no, because each hour given to someone else's request is an hour taken from something else. When Lina agreed out of habit she was often refusing the things she cared about most: rest, her own projects, even a quiet evening with a book. The habit of yes, so respectable on the surface, was quietly emptying her own life.

Rosa gave her a simple sentence that she could use anywhere: let me think about it and I will come back to you. It broke the automatic link between a request and a yes, and it gave Lina the time she needed to ask herself what she really wanted. Many of her old commitments, she noticed, would never have been made if she had paused for a single night.

Lina decided to begin with the smallest no she could find, and the opportunity came on Monday when a colleague asked her to take over a routine task. She said that she was sorry but she was not able to this time, and her heart thudded as though she had run up a flight of stairs. The colleague simply shrugged, said it was no problem and turned to ask someone else.

Rosa taught her a simple formula for a kind refusal: thank the person, say no clearly, and stop. There is no need for an elaborate excuse, she explained, because a long justification only gives the other person something to argue with, whereas a short and friendly answer is much harder to dispute. Lina practised in front of the mirror until the words sounded less like an apology and more like a decision.

Not everyone took her refusals gracefully, and one friend sulked for an entire week. Rosa reminded her that a person's disappointment is an emotion growing in their own garden, and that they are entirely capable of tending it without Lina rushing in to pull it up. You can regret that someone is unhappy, she said, without being responsible for making them happy.

After her refusals, Lina was often overwhelmed by a wave of guilt that made her want to take everything back. Rosa told her that guilt is a feeling rather than a verdict, and that the useful question is whether she had actually done something wrong or merely something unfamiliar. In most cases, she suggested, the guilt was only the discomfort of a new habit.

Lina's mother loved her deeply and worried about her constantly, and she had always hoped that her daughter would keep her steady position at the insurance office. A secure job, in her view, was the best protection against the troubles she had known in her own life. Lina understood this perfectly, and the understanding made the matter harder rather than easier, because she could not even be angry with her mother.

Rosa told her that she could love her mother dearly and still choose a different road, since respect and obedience are two quite different things. A parent's advice deserves to be heard with care, but a grown daughter remains the only person who has to live with the consequences. Lina found that she could honour her mother's love without handing over the steering wheel.

One evening Lina sat down with her mother and, instead of arguing or hiding, explained calmly what she wanted and why she had thought about it for months. She thanked her mother for the worry behind her advice and promised to be careful with her decisions. It was not an easy conversation, and her mother cried a little, but nothing between them was broken.

Lina came to understand that her mother's objections were not a wish to control her but a form of fear, and that fear is often what love looks like when it is frightened. Over the following weeks her mother gradually softened, began to ask questions about Lina's plans and even offered, grudgingly, to look at a sketch. Not every parent responds so generously, Rosa remarked, but it is always worth giving them the chance.

Lina had a habit of checking the number of likes on her photographs within minutes of posting them, and her mood rose and fell with the count. Rosa observed that the platforms turn opinion into a number, which is a very poor instrument for measuring the worth of a person or a day. A like, she said, costs the giver a fraction of a second, so it ought not to be allowed to buy so much of your peace.

Lina often felt that other people's lives were shinier and more successful than her own, until Rosa pointed out the flaw in the comparison. People tend to display their finest moments and hide the untidy ones, so we end up comparing our own behind-the-scenes footage with their carefully edited trailers. The contest, Rosa remarked, is rigged from the start, and there is no shame in declining to enter it.

One afternoon Rosa told Lina her own story, which she rarely did, and she told it simply. As a young woman she had been advised on every side that tailoring was not a proper job for a clever girl, and several relatives had refused to speak to her for a year. She had gone ahead regardless, trembling at times, and she had not regretted it for a single day.

Rosa gave her three questions to ask whenever criticism arrived: who is saying this, do they really know me, and is any of it useful? A comment from a stranger who knew nothing of her life could be put down quite quickly, while a remark from someone who understood her deserved careful attention. The questions turned a frightening flood of judgement into something she could sort and sift.

Lina worried that her new independence might turn her into someone who ignored everybody, but Rosa assured her that it was nothing of the kind. Wise advice is a gift, and the free person is simply the one who listens, weighs it honestly and then makes her own decision instead of obeying by reflex. To be free of opinions, Rosa said, is not to be deaf to them.

Lina had always assumed that honesty and kindness pulled in opposite directions, so she had chosen kindness and sacrificed the truth. Rosa showed her that a true statement, delivered gently and at a suitable moment, can honour both the listener and the speaker. Kindness without honesty, she said, is merely politeness, and honesty without kindness is mere noise.

Rosa asked her a simple question that nobody had ever put to her: what really matters to you? After a long and difficult silence, Lina wrote five words on a card, and they included honesty, creativity, kindness, health and family. It was strange to see on paper something she had never been allowed, or had never allowed herself, to decide.

Values, Rosa said, work like a compass: they do not tell you where every path leads, but they show which way is north. Whenever Lina faced a difficult choice, she held it up against her five words and asked whether the decision pointed towards them or away. Often the answer came more quickly than she expected, and it came from her own voice rather than from the crowd.

Lina's deepest fear, she realised, was being disliked, and Rosa advised her to approach it as one approaches cold water, a little at a time. She chose small, manageable tests, such as disagreeing politely in a meeting or giving an honest opinion about a film, and each one made the fear a little less enormous. Courage, Rosa said, is not the absence of fear but the habit of doing the next small thing anyway.

At a dinner with friends, where she would once have agreed with the majority, Lina said honestly which film she preferred, and it was not the popular choice. She waited for a storm that did not come, and one friend even admitted that she had secretly wanted the same film. Honest opinions, offered lightly, are often a relief to everyone, because many people are hiding behind the same polite silence.

Rosa offered a hard truth that was oddly liberating: some people will dislike you whatever you do, however kind, careful and agreeable you try to be. Pleasing everyone is not a difficult goal but an impossible one, because tastes and moods differ and some people simply decide not to like us. Once Lina accepted this, she found that a great deal of her exhausting effort fell quietly away.

Lina observed with some surprise that her closest friends took her new honesty in their stride, and several said they were glad to know what she really thought. Real friendship, she realised, is not an exchange of constant agreement but a relationship in which each person is allowed to be fully themselves. The people who truly care, Rosa said, stay when you start telling the truth.

Not every relationship survived the change, and Lina's friend Mei, who had always relied on her agreeableness, gradually stopped calling. It hurt, and Lina was tempted to return to her old habits in order to win her back, but she recognised that the friendship had been built on a version of herself that no longer existed. She allowed herself to feel sad for a while and did not pretend to be indifferent, which, she found, was the quickest way through.

Rosa told her that grief is the natural price of change and that there was no need to hurry past it or to feel ashamed of it. After a week of sadness, Lina noticed that her days had more time in them, her conversations more truth and her evenings more peace than she had known for years. The loss was real, but so was the gain, and she could hold both at once.

Rosa reminded her that her own garden needed daily attention, and that the freedom she wanted would not arrive in one dramatic leap. Each morning Lina chose one small task that belonged only to her, such as a walk, a drawing or an honest message, and she completed it with care. A life, Rosa said, is made of such small acts, and it is steered by them.

Lina liked to explain her timidity by pointing to her childhood, and there was truth in the explanation, though Rosa gently refused to let it become an excuse. The past, she said, can explain a great deal about why we are as we are, but it does not hold the pen when we write the next page. This was a challenging thought, but it was also a hopeful one, because it meant that nothing had been settled for ever.

Every real choice, Rosa pointed out, comes with consequences, and some of them will be unwelcome to someone, so there is no point in waiting for a decision that nobody will mind. Having thought carefully, Lina chose to enrol in an evening class in clothes design, taught on Tuesdays near Mill Lane, and she signed the form with a hand that shook only slightly. It was, she noted, the first thing she had done in years purely because she wanted to.

On the first evening of the class Lina arrived early and sat nervously among the strangers, convinced that every pair of eyes was assessing her. In reality the other students were absorbed in their own fabrics and their own anxieties, and one or two actually smiled at her as she threaded her machine. The spotlight, Lina remembered with a private smile, was mostly in her own imagination, and it could be switched off at will.

Her first sleeve came out lopsided, and for a few seconds Lina felt her face burn as she waited for someone to mock it. Instead the woman beside her laughed in a friendly way, admitted that her own first sleeve had looked like a sausage, and showed her how to unpick it. The embarrassment, Lina noticed, passed within minutes, leaving behind only a little more skill.

At the office, Lina made an appointment with her manager, Mr Hale, and prepared carefully for what she wanted to say. She explained, politely and without apology, that she had been taking on far too many tasks and wished to agree on a workload she could manage well. It was one of the most frightening conversations of her life, and she carried it out with a steady voice.

Mr Hale looked surprised and a little thoughtful, and for a moment Lina was certain that she had made a terrible mistake. Then he said that he had assumed she was happy to do everything, agreed to hand some of her duties to others and suggested that they review the arrangement in a month. The result was a compromise rather than a victory, but it was a good deal better than silence.

Not everybody welcomed the change, and one colleague, who had grown used to handing Lina her tedious tasks, was visibly irritated. Lina felt the old discomfort rise, but she remembered the two gardens and remained courteous without giving way. It was the first time she had stood her ground without feeling that she had committed a crime.

As the weeks passed, Lina became aware of something new growing inside her, a quiet and rather solid respect for herself. It was not pride, and it was certainly not arrogance, but a simple sense that she mattered and that her life was hers to steer. She no longer needed everyone's approval to feel that she had a right to be here.

Lina made a scarf for an elderly neighbour who had been kind to her, and the experience was entirely different from her old pleasing. She gave it because she wanted to, not because she feared the consequences of refusing, and the delight on the old woman's face was something she could enjoy without anxiety. Generosity that is freely chosen, she discovered, nourishes the giver as well as the receiver.

Rosa told her that being liked is pleasant but fragile, whereas being trusted is solid and lasts, and that the two are not always the same thing. People trust those who tell the truth, keep their word and treat others fairly, even when what they say is not what anyone wants to hear. Lina decided that she would rather be trusted by a few than flattered by many.

A year after that first lopsided sleeve, Lina finished a coat that she had designed and sewn entirely by herself, in a deep green wool with oversized buttons. Rosa hung it in the window of the shop on Mill Lane, and passers-by stopped to look at it, some frowning and some smiling. Lina watched them from across the street and found, to her great pleasure, that she was happy either way.

On the last evening of the year, Rosa summed up what they had learned in a few plain sentences, which Lina wrote at the top of a new notebook. Tend your own garden with care, let other people tend theirs, listen to good advice without obeying it blindly, and be honest and kind in the same breath. Freedom from other people's opinions, she said, is not a place you reach once but a way of walking that you practise every day.
